conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/name: Heraclius' war with Persia and the True Cross
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/religion: The war began as a great-power conflict: Khosrow II invaded in 603 claiming to avenge his patron, the murdered emperor Maurice, and the stakes were territory, tribute and survival. Religion became major after the Persian capture of Jerusalem in 614 and the removal of the relic of the True Cross to Ctesiphon. Heraclius' counter-offensives of 622–628 were accompanied by icons, sermons and the destruction of Zoroastrian fire temples, and his return of the Cross to Jerusalem in 630 was celebrated as a religious triumph. Some historians have called this the 'first crusade'; Walter Kaegi and James Howard-Johnston are more cautious, stressing Heraclius' strategic brilliance and diplomacy and noting that much of the religious colouring comes from later chroniclers such as Theophanes and from court poetry. The Persian side was not waging a religious war against Christianity as such: Khosrow had Christian wives and advisers and many of his subjects belonged to the Church of the East.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/sides/0/: Chalcedonian Christianity, with large Miaphysite populations in Syria and Egypt
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/sides/1/: Zoroastrianism (state religion), with large Christian (Church of the East and Miaphysite) and Jewish minorities
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/summary: The last and greatest war between Rome and Persia lasted a quarter of a century. Persian armies overran Syria, Palestine and Egypt, took Jerusalem in 614 and carried off the True Cross, and with the Avars besieged Constantinople in 626. Heraclius turned the war around with bold campaigns through Armenia and the Caucasus, destroyed the great Zoroastrian fire temple at Ganzak, crushed a Persian army near Nineveh in 627 and forced a peace in 628. He returned the Cross to Jerusalem in 630, only for both exhausted empires to face the Arab conquests within a few years.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/story:
In 602 the emperor Maurice, who had restored Khosrow II to the Persian throne in 591, was overthrown and murdered with his sons by the centurion Phocas. Khosrow declared war in 603, claiming to avenge his benefactor, and paraded a pretender said to be Maurice's son. Phocas' unpopular regime struggled; Persian armies took the Roman fortress of Dara in 604 and pushed into Armenia and Anatolia. In 610 Heraclius, son of the exarch of Carthage, sailed from Africa, overthrew and executed Phocas, and became emperor, but for years he could not stop the Persian advance.

The Persians took Antioch in 613 and Damascus soon after. In spring 614 the general Shahrbaraz besieged Jerusalem; after about three weeks the walls were breached. The monk Strategius, an eyewitness, describes days of slaughter of Christians, the burning of churches including the Holy Sepulchre, and the deportation of the patriarch Zacharias and many captives to Persia, together with the relic of the True Cross. Local Jews, who had suffered under Christian rule and had been briefly allowed to govern the city by the Persians, were blamed by Christian writers for part of the killing; the scale of the massacre in Strategius' figures is not trusted, but excavated mass burials in Jerusalem confirm heavy loss of life. Egypt, the empire's granary, fell between 618 and 621, and a Persian army camped at Chalcedon within sight of Constantinople.

Heraclius gave the struggle a sacred character. With the church's consent he melted down church plate to pay his troops, and in 622 he left the capital carrying an icon of Christ 'not made by human hands', addressing his army as men fighting for God and for the captive Christians. In campaigns of 622–625 he manoeuvred through Anatolia and Armenia, and in 623 or 624 he sacked Ganzak and destroyed the great fire temple of Adur Gushnasp at Takht-i Suleiman in retaliation for Jerusalem. He wintered in Albania (in the Caucasus) and allied with the Western Turks, who ravaged Persian territory and besieged Tiflis.

In the summer of 626, while Heraclius remained in the East, a huge Avar and Slav host besieged Constantinople from the European side as a Persian army under Shahrbaraz waited across the Bosporus. The patriarch Sergius led processions with the icon of the Virgin round the walls, and when the Avar assault and the Slav canoe fleet failed in early August the defenders attributed their deliverance to the Theotokos; the hymn known as the Akathist became associated with the victory. Heraclius' brother Theodore defeated another Persian army in Anatolia.

In autumn 627 Heraclius invaded Mesopotamia from the Caucasus with Turkic support. On 12 December he defeated the Persian army under Rhahzadh near the ruins of Nineveh, killing its commander in single combat according to the chronicles. He went on to sack Khosrow's palace at Dastagird. Khosrow's authority collapsed: in February 628 he was deposed and murdered by his son Kavad II (Shiroe), who made peace on the basis of the old frontiers, prisoners released and the Cross returned. Persia then fell into civil war, with several rulers in four years.

After negotiations with Shahrbaraz, who briefly seized the Persian throne, the relic of the Cross was restored. Heraclius brought it into Jerusalem in a solemn procession, traditionally on 21 March 630, the origin of the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross associated with his name in the West. The victory was followed by reprisals: Jews were expelled from Jerusalem and many killed, and in 632 Heraclius ordered the forced baptism of Jews in the empire. In the same years he and Patriarch Sergius sought to reunite Miaphysite Christians through the formulas of Monoenergism and later Monothelitism, which caused new division. Within a decade of the triumph Arab Muslim armies, facing two drained empires, took Syria, Palestine and Egypt from Byzantium (Yarmuk 636, Jerusalem 637/638) and destroyed the Sasanian state.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/nameOfGo: Heraclius' campaigns were framed as a war for Christ and the captive Cross. He carried the icon of Christ 'not made by hands' (the acheiropoietos image), was praised by the court poet George of Pisidia as a new David and Heraclius-Hercules fighting the fire-worshippers, and according to Theophanes urged his soldiers to win the crown of martyrdom. The destruction of the Zoroastrian fire temple at Ganzak was presented as revenge for the burning of Jerusalem. In Constantinople in 626 Patriarch Sergius processed the icons of Christ and the Virgin round the walls, and victory was credited to the Theotokos. The restoration of the True Cross to Jerusalem in 630 was a deliberate religious ceremony of triumph.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/religiou: The capture of Jerusalem in 614, the burning of churches and the removal of the True Cross to Persia gave the war a sacred cause for Roman Christians.
Byzantine imperial ideology held the emperor to be the protector of Christendom and of the holy places.
Christian–Jewish tensions in Palestine shaped the violence of 614 and the reprisals of 629–632.
Sasanian kings used Zoroastrian kingship ideology, and fire temples were symbolic targets for Heraclius.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/otherCau: Centuries of Roman–Persian rivalry over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the frontier fortresses.
Khosrow II's opportunistic claim to avenge Maurice after Phocas' coup of 602.
Internal Byzantine instability under Phocas and civil war in 608–610 that weakened the eastern defences.
The ambitions of Khosrow II to restore the Achaemenid empire's boundaries, and the wealth of Syria and Egypt.
Steppe politics: the Avars' pressure on the Balkans and the Western Turks' readiness to ally with Constantinople.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/triggers: The murder of the emperor Maurice and his sons by Phocas in November 602.
The Persian capture of Jerusalem and the True Cross in 614, which transformed the war's meaning for Christians.
Heraclius' departure from Constantinople on campaign at Easter 622.

conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/casualti: No reliable overall estimate exists for a war of twenty-six years fought across the Near East. Strategius' account gives tens of thousands of Christian dead at Jerusalem in 614, a figure modern historians regard as inflated, though mass graves found at Mamilla and elsewhere confirm large-scale killing. Losses from famine, plague, deportation and the Avar and Turkic raids cannot be quantified.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/effects/: Byzantium recovered its eastern provinces and the Cross, but both empires were financially, militarily and demographically exhausted.
The Sasanian state collapsed into civil war after 628, opening the way for its conquest by the Arabs in the 630s–650s.
The Arab Muslim conquest of Syria, Palestine and Egypt followed within a decade of Heraclius' triumph.
Jewish communities in Palestine suffered reprisals and Heraclius decreed forced baptism in 632.
Heraclius' reign marks the transition from the late Roman to the medieval Byzantine state, with Greek replacing Latin in government.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/effectsO: The cult of the True Cross was strengthened; the West later linked the feast of the Exaltation (14 September) to Heraclius' restoration.
The Virgin was celebrated as protector of Constantinople, and the Akathist hymn became tied to the deliverance of 626.
Heraclius' attempt to win back Miaphysites through Monoenergism and Monothelitism produced the controversy settled at the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681).
The war's devastation weakened Chalcedonian Christianity in Syria and Egypt just before the Arab conquests.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/legacy: Medieval Western writers made Heraclius a model crusader: his recovery of the Cross was read in sermons and appeared in the Golden Legend, and some crusade preachers invoked him. Modern historians debate whether the war deserves the title of the first holy war of Christendom. Its greater legacy is ironic: the triumph of 628–630 left Rome and Persia too exhausted to resist the new power that emerged from Arabia.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/dissente: In a letter from Africa, Maximus expressed dismay at the forced baptism of Jews ordered by Heraclius in 632, fearing that compelled baptism defiled the sacrament and would produce false conversions.
Christians of the Church of the East

Many Christians within the Persian empire served Khosrow loyally and did not regard the war as a struggle between Christ and Zoroaster, a reminder that the Christian world was itself divided by the conflict.
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/theatres: Jerusalem, sack and capture of the Cross
Ganzak and the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp (Takht-i Suleiman)
conflicts/heraclius-persian-war/campaign: The Persian conquest of the Roman East, 613–619
Persian armies under Shahrbaraz and Shahin
After defeating Heraclius near Antioch the Persians took Damascus, moved down the coast, captured Jerusalem in May 614 and carried the Cross east, then invaded Egypt and took Alexandria.
Heraclius with Roman troops and Turkic allies

From the Black Sea and the Caucasus Heraclius joined the Turks before Tiflis, marched south through the Zagros, destroyed the Persian field army near Nineveh, sacked Dastagird and approached Ctesiphon, triggering Khosrow's overthrow.
The return of the True Cross, 630
After receiving the relic from the Persians, Heraclius travelled through Syria and Galilee and entered Jerusalem in procession to restore the Cross to the Holy Sepulchre.
